The "mom-cession" is also happening for women without college degrees who have young kids at home.

Rising unemployment
Declining participation

For moms without college degrees, the biggest declines are in retail and education.

posts.text:
What a chart...
The labor market is getting worse for American moms.

Unemployment for college-educated moms of young kids keeps rising.
Employment-to-population ratio is way down

"Mom-cession" ?
Return to office is likely part of the story.
Expensive childcare another part of the story.
It's interesting to see the big drop off in college educated moms of young kids employed in healthcare/social assistance and education.

Important charts from @MattNestlerPhD

posts.text:
Gas prices are back below $4 for the first time since March 30.

The AAA average gas price fell to $3.999 today. 
That's still a dollar above where gas prices were before the war in Iran began. But it's a psychological milestone to see prices drop below $4 again

Warning: Getting back below $3.50 could be harder. In 2022, it took until after Thanksgiving to get back below $3.50

-1 rate hike by year-end
-Slightly slower GDP growth for 2026

posts.text:
Wow. I just got my latest electric bill.

Exact same daily usage as last year
Exact same daily avg. temp as last year
But... a nearly 30% increase in the daily avg. cost

(The official CPI report says electricity costs are up 6% in the past year. Obviously, it varies by region)

posts.text:
Inflation is so high that it's erasing all wage gains.

Inflation: 4.2% in May for the past year
Wage growth: 3.4% in May for the past year.

Americans are getting squeezed financially. This isn't just "bad vibes" about the economy. There is real pain, especially for middle-class and lower-income households. It's tough because so many basic items are seeing sizable price increases: gas, electricity, food, medical care.

posts.text:
JUST IN: US inflation jumped to 4.2% (y/y) in May —>the highest in 3 years and up from 2.4% in February before the war in Iran.

Higher gas and energy prices drove 60% of the gain. Shelter and food (especially restaurants) also contributed. The monthly increase was 0.5%.

Core inflation (excluding food and energy) was 2.9% —>highest since September
